headline: Nvidia's leadership crisis is the day's dominant story, with the board weighing CEO Jensen Huang's future and pulling AI stocks lower, while hot US inflation keeps a Fed rate-hike narrative alive and Anthropic's IPO draws scrutiny. In healthcare, Pfizer's $1.5 billion Blackstone co-funding deal for its obesity drug stands out.
watch: Nvidia board decision on Jensen Huang and the stock's reaction at the open
Fed speakers and rate-hike pricing ahead of the December meeting, with the dollar near a 19-month high

paragraphs.text: The biggest financing story is Pfizer's agreement with Blackstone Life Sciences for up to $1.5 billion to help fund development of berobenatide, an obesity candidate. The WSJ, Endpoints and Fierce Biotech all report it. Fierce describes the drug as a monthly GLP-1 receptor agonist, and Endpoints ties it to the ex-Metsera asset. For an investor, this is a large pharma using outside structured capital to share the cost of a late obesity push rather than carrying it all on its own balance sheet. The headlines give no terms on returns or royalties.

paragraphs.text: Venture and M&A activity stayed busy. Neurosterix, an Addex spinout, raised a $105 million Series B for a schizophrenia drug. Endpoints notes that former Cobenfy figures are involved and that the candidate hits one of the targets of Bristol Myers Squibb's drug. Fierce says the money funds a planned Phase 2 trial. VectorY added $83.5 million to its Series A for brain-delivered antibody gene therapies. Flagship Pioneering is merging two of its AI-focused startups, Valo Health and Montai Therapeutics. AstraZeneca bought the vaccine startup Omniose, which BioPharma Dive says gives it a simpler way to make conjugate vaccines. BioNTech paid $205 million for an FDA priority review voucher to speed a late-stage oncology filing. In behavioral health, XRHealth acquired PursueCare.

paragraphs.text: On the clinical and regulatory side, STAT says Biogen is expected to release pivotal lupus trial results soon, and that readout could move the stock. Beeline Medicines also fleshed out Phase 2 lupus data from a former Bristol Myers drug, calling it an impressive win that sets up Phase 3. Amgen shared detailed Phase 3 Sjögren's data ahead of what Fierce calls a showdown with Novartis. J&J posted a second Phase 3 bipolar mania win for Caplyta and is preparing a label expansion. Merck KGaA won FDA approval for a licensed tumor drug for a rare joint condition, which Fierce says sets up competition with Ono and Daiichi. The market punished some names, though. ImmunityBio fell about 20% despite a Phase 3 bladder cancer win because of thin data and weak quarterly financials. Legend Biotech dropped 16% after its first report under its new CEO. Summit Therapeutics is losing commercial leaders ahead of the FDA decision on ivonescimab. STAT also argues Alnylam depends heavily on Amvuttra, whose sales growth has slowed.

paragraphs.text: Consumer and digital health keeps pulling in capital. Oura will pay $625 million for the AI virtual primary care firm Counsel Health, one more wearable maker pushing into clinical services. Hims & Hers reported $890.4 million of third-quarter revenue and a $33 million net loss, against a $15.8 million profit a year ago. It also tightened its 2026 outlook, and Endpoints says it is now leaning on brand-name drugs and pharma partners. NYT DealBook says Ro's annualized revenue has grown nearly tenfold since it embraced GLP-1 treatments. Google Cloud launched a healthcare version of Gemini, and AWS committed $100 million over five years to health AI and cloud initiatives.

paragraphs.text: Policy and provider news was mixed. STAT reports drugmakers are looking for ways to protect US sales from the administration's most-favored-nation pricing policy, including rethinking launches abroad. BioPharma Dive cites a study saying German drug price increases could push US costs higher, amid friction over pricing. NYT says hospitals are bracing for Medicaid work rules starting Jan. 1 and for deep funding cuts. Two US senators have asked HHS how it is handling risks from prediction markets tied to clinical trials and approvals. Carelon agreed to pay more than $10 million to settle New York allegations over mental health networks and coverage denials. UnitedHealth added a children's hospital executive to its board, and BJC Health and St. Luke's signed a letter of intent to merge. Coverage of insurers and hospitals was light on financial detail today.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia is moving the whole tape. The FT, NYT and MarketWatch report that its board is considering Jensen Huang's future after reports of a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence reportedly judged to be a spy. A second report, in NYT, describes a relationship with an executive who reports to him. The stock fell more than 8% after hours and was down almost 6% before the open, per the FT. Nasdaq futures dropped about 1%, which WSJ says put the brakes on an AI rally. Baird downgraded the stock to neutral and cut its price target, citing worries about Huang and AI uncertainty. CNBC cites analysts saying shares could drop 20% or more if he leaves, and the FT says a Huang-less Nvidia would probably lose some market share and pricing power. All of this rests on reports of board deliberations, not an announced decision, so the next hours matter.

paragraphs.text: The fallout reaches Washington and Beijing. The FT says Huang is losing favor in Washington. NYT reports that Treasury Secretary Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Lutnick over why advanced chip sales to Megaspeed had not been restricted. MarketWatch says Megaspeed has issued its first public statement. China has warned the US not to use the episode as a pretext for tech curbs, and CNBC says the Ministry of State Security is now in the spotlight. Some Silicon Valley figures, including Elon Musk, are defending Huang as a personal lapse and not a security failure. The risk for investors is that a governance story turns into export-control policy.

paragraphs.text: The wider AI trade is wobbling. CoreWeave surged after earnings on Wednesday and lifted the Nasdaq, per CNBC, but WSJ says European stocks opened higher on a rotation away from AI. FT pieces describe mounting concentration risk in the AI megatrade, and WSJ notes that an AI bust would spill beyond the US, with parts of Asia seen as heavily exposed to the data-center build-out. Wellington-Altus's Jim Thorne expects a violent tech bounce but warns against chasing it. CNBC offers themes beyond Nvidia, including cybersecurity, robotics and quantum computing.

paragraphs.text: Rates and currencies are driven by inflation. CNBC says October CPI came in above expectations, and Fed's Goolsbee called it borderline disturbing. WSJ reports two Fed officials suggesting the pace of hikes may need to quicken before the December meeting. The dollar hit a 19-month high, the yen fell to two-month lows, and Treasury yields rose while European yields fell. ING flags a risk of the euro falling below $1.10. Elsewhere, UK third-quarter GDP grew 0.7%, the strongest quarter since early 2024, helped by AI investment. The FT says that alone won't push the Bank of England to move in December, while the NIESR think tank wants the rate at around 5%. A BOJ board member urged caution on further hikes, and the PBoC kept an accommodative stance. The FT also reports France backing Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos for ECB president.

paragraphs.text: Corporate results were uneven. Yeti cut its sales growth outlook to about 6%, from 7% to 8%, on consumer caution, while Burberry rose more than 9% on higher retail sales. SMIC doubled its profit on AI-related demand. Rolls-Royce set a $2 billion buyback, part of up to about $12 billion through 2028, and BAE raised its cash flow guidance again. Telefonica lifted earnings guidance but cut its revenue target. Hapag-Lloyd is still benefiting from higher freight rates, and Endeavour Mining fell sharply on lower-end production guidance. MSCI ruled Strategy, the biggest corporate bitcoin holder, ineligible for its indexes. Separately, NYT reports that Kalshi and the CFTC are allowing perpetual trades on stocks and crypto, drawing lawsuits from two clearinghouses.

NYT also asks whether the voter backlash could help the economy. NYT says heating costs will rise 7% on average this winter, with heating oil up around 70% because of the Iran war.

paragraphs.text: The most striking credit item is Bloomberg's report on about $22 billion of US bank preferred shares, which have fallen harder this year than even the riskiest junk bonds, leaving holders with no good way out. These are usually seen as income paper, so a drawdown worse than junk is notable. The headline gives no cause, so treat it as a warning about liquidity and positioning rather than a verdict on bank credit.

paragraphs.text: Leverage and AI financing are the other themes. The Financial Stability Board is preparing a consultation on how to gather data on hedge funds' leveraged bond bets, after earlier transparency efforts were hampered by differing definitions and limits on cross-border data sharing. Morgan Stanley, per CNBC, tells investors to stick with high-quality hyperscaler bonds, seeing a more attractive entry point even as worries over AI debt persist. WSJ says CoreWeave is balancing capital needs against its data-center expansion, but the blurb carries no detail.

paragraphs.text: Private credit is spreading and drawing attention abroad. In Australia, La Trobe Private Credit Fund applied to quote 83,782 units, and ASIC released a report following its surveillance of private credit funds, though the summary says little about findings. Saudi Venture Capital invested in Jadwa's private credit fund, and a Bloomberg Invest Dubai panel on private credit and secondaries framed slower exits and tighter financing as reshaping valuations. Sri Lanka's private credit reached Rs.2.1 trillion, with short-term loans taking a bigger share. South Korea's FSS warned securities firms over high-yield promissory notes. In the US, Simply Wall St asks whether record earnings changed the story for Trinity Capital, a lender.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is the main deal story, and the coverage is skeptical. Bloomberg says AI doubts are colliding with the mega-IPO, and the FT says the company is pressing ahead despite adversity for the broader AI trade. FT Alphaville calls the deal too important to fail. It expects huge demand and a blockbuster debut, but warns that shadow insider sales and circular supply-chain backing could cause after-market indigestion. NYT DealBook notes that some of the biggest IPO investors are also key business partners. Morningstar says the listing won't dramatically change the stock market but will increase concentration. Other pieces compare it with the biggest US IPOs and look at backers' stakes at the midpoint, though the blurbs here give no figures I can confirm. The circularity between investors and suppliers is the point to watch when books open.

An FT Alphaville piece sharply criticizes the Enforcement Division. Fewer actions could reduce deal and disclosure friction for issuers. It could also raise reputational or litigation risks elsewhere. The headlines do not say which.
